<reason>Both sides opened strongly with concrete, plausible examples and a clear normative frame, but CON (A) executed the later rounds more precisely. CON's sustained ex ante/ex post distinction (enumerated statutes name protected conduct before anyone acts; a "materially affects" standard only resolves after litigation) gave the judge a clean, consistent metric that PRO's own hard cases kept illustrating. The decisive moment came when PRO, answering CON's pressure question, said employers could act on "reasonable, good-faith business judgment"—a standard CON correctly pointed out is nowhere in the motion's text, which protects conduct that "objectively" does not materially affect performance. CON's closing pressed this inconsistency hard ("a rule that needs rewriting to be defended is a draft, not a standard"), and PRO's closing pivoted to a "speculative vs. real harm" framing without ever repairing that specific textual gap. PRO's rebuttals were competent—turning CON's examples into confirmations of the standard, and exposing weak spots in CON's mutuality argument—but PRO never fully neutralized CON's core administrability critique or the good-faith/objective-standard tension, leaving CON's throughline more intact at the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 (A4.5) catching PRO's Pressure-Question answer ("reasonable, good-faith business judgment") as inconsistent with the motion's objective "does not materially affect" text—a gotcha PRO's closing never directly repaired.</best_rebuttal>
